Discouraged
dis-KUR-ijd
v. (past part.)
From dis- (privative) and courage, Old French corage, from Latin cor, the heart. Webster 1828: deprived of courage; depressed in spirits; disheartened. Literally, un-hearted — the heart taken out of a man.

Biblical Definition

Discouraged is literally to have the heart taken out, and Scripture records it of a nation, warns fathers against causing it in children, and denies it of the Messiah. Of the nation: they journeyed from mount Hor by the way of the Red sea, to compass the land of Edom: and the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way (Numbers 21:4). It was not the enemy that unhearted them but the route — a detour around Edom, going backward toward the sea they had already crossed — and the murmuring and the fiery serpents follow immediately. Moses had earlier put the command in the plainest terms at the border: Behold, the LORD thy God hath set the land before thee: go up and possess it… fear not, neither be discouraged (Deuteronomy 1:21). Paul names it as the specific damage a father can do: Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged (Colossians 3:21) — the danger to a child under a harsh father is not rebellion but the loss of heart. And Isaiah says of the Servant that He alone will not suffer it: He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law (Isaiah 42:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DISCOURAGED as deprived of courage; disheartened; depressed in spirits; deterred or dissuaded from an undertaking by fear or difficulty.

expand to see more

DISCOURAGED, pp. — Deprived of courage; disheartened; depressed in spirits.

Deterred or dissuaded from an attempt by fear, difficulty, or the appearance of danger.

Deprived of confidence in the success of an undertaking; dispirited.

Applied to individuals, to armies, and to whole peoples whose resolution has failed.

From dis- and courage, from Latin cor, the heart — the root also of cordial, concord, and record.

Key Scripture

Numbers 21:4 — "And they journeyed from mount Hor by the way of the Red sea, to compass the land of Edom: and the soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way."

Deuteronomy 1:21 — "Behold, the LORD thy God hath set the land before thee: go up and possess it, as the LORD God of thy fathers hath said unto thee; fear not, neither be discouraged."

Colossians 3:21 — "Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged."

Isaiah 42:4 — "He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law."

Modern Corruption

Colossians 3:21 addresses fathers by name and warns of a specific injury — a child un-hearted by provocation — and both the harsh reading of headship that ignores the warning and the abdicating father who reads it as a reason to command nothing miss what Paul wrote.

expand to see more

The verse is addressed to fathers, not to parents generally, and it sits immediately after Children, obey your parents in all things. Paul gives authority and then bounds it, which is the invariable biblical pattern for every office. The injury he names is not resentment but discouragement: a child who has been provoked long enough does not fight, he gives up, and Ephesians 6:4 gives the positive alternative — bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. A complementarian household that quotes the command to children and passes over the command to fathers has taken half a text. The dictionary holds the creational order of headship without reservation and holds this warning with equal force, because Paul joined them in one paragraph.

The opposite failure is now the more common one. Reading the warning as though any exercise of paternal authority risks damaging a child, many fathers command nothing, correct nothing, and leave their households to be discipled by whatever else is available. That is not the avoidance of provocation; it is the abdication Eli was judged for, whose sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not (1 Samuel 3:13). Numbers 21:4 shows the third and quieter source of discouragement, which no one causes: the way itself. Israel lost heart not at a battle but at a detour, which is worth remembering by anyone whose present trouble is merely that the road has gone on longer than expected.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qatsar (H7114), to be short, shortened — the soul of the people was shortened; chathath (H2865), to be broken, dismayed; Greek athumeo (G120), to be disheartened, literally without spirit.

expand to see more

Hebrew qatsar (H7114) — to be short, impatient; Numbers 21:4 says literally that the soul of the people was shortened by the way.

Hebrew chathath (H2865) — to be dismayed, broken, shattered; fear not, neither be discouraged (Deuteronomy 1:21).

Hebrew ratsats (H7533) — to crush, to break; He shall not fail in Isaiah 42:4 is from this root, echoing the bruised reed of verse 3.

Greek athumeo (G120) — to be without heart or spirit, to lose courage; only at Colossians 3:21.

Greek ekkakeo (G1573) — to faint, to lose heart; let us not be weary in well doing (Galatians 6:9).

Usage

"The soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way (Numbers 21:4) — unhearted by a detour, not by an enemy."

"Fathers, provoke not your children… lest they be discouraged (Colossians 3:21) — authority given and then bounded."

"He shall not fail nor be discouraged (Isaiah 42:4) — said of the Servant alone."
